blockers: The Commodity Promotion, Research, and Information Act and the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act set how such programs continue or end, and the termination found followed the Act's referendum rule, so ending programs by administrative choice appears limited (inference).
Elimination of checkoffs or marketing orders in general, or a mandatory five-year vote, would require Congress.
Congress is moving to extend at least one checkoff (dairy) in both 2026 farm bill vehicles.
No USDA or congressional initiative to curtail these programs generally was found.
confidence_reason: Federal Register records confirm that the one termination and one withdrawal followed producer votes under existing law and that other AMS actions went the other way at industry request, and the House checkoff bill contains no elimination or periodic-vote provision. The absence of a USDA or congressional initiative is still an absence-of-evidence finding.

durability.why: The paper packaging termination is a final rule that removed the order from the CFR, but a new industry request could create a program again, and the rest of the program structure is unchanged.

est_completion.basis: Inference: the only terminations found followed industry votes, no USDA initiative or bill to eliminate programs was found, and elimination or mandatory voting would need legislation.

proposal: The Mandate calls marketing orders and checkoff programs compelled-funding arrangements and recommends that USDA reduce their number and scope, reject new requests where the law allows, eliminate existing programs when possible, make it easier for affected parties to end them, and reject any return of volume controls. It also recommends working with Congress to eliminate them, or at least to require a vote of affected parties at least every five years that USDA must honor.
remaining: A general USDA effort to reduce the number and scope of checkoff programs and marketing orders and to reject new requests (p. 306): none found; the terminations and withdrawals found followed producer votes under existing statutes, and several AMS actions (Christmas tree expense cap, proposed South Texas onion amendments) went the other way at industry request.

Easier termination and a USDA duty to honor termination requests (p. 306): none found; the South Texas onion proposal would lower the share needed to continue that order, which is the reverse direction.

Legislation to eliminate marketing orders and checkoffs or to require votes at least every five years (p. 306): none found; the checkoff bills found (H.R. 3516, S. 1848) are transparency and lobbying bills.
Volume controls (p. 306): a marketing order with supply regulation, spearmint oil, was still being implemented in 2026.

status_summary: As of 2026-10-08 no USDA or congressional initiative was found to reduce the number of marketing orders and checkoff programs, reject new requests, ease termination, eliminate the programs, or require periodic votes. The reductions found came from producer-initiated processes under existing law: after a petition from more than 10 percent of eligible voters in January 2025 and a referendum in July 2025 (about 73.5 percent of voters, about 90.4 percent of volume, favoring termination), AMS terminated the paper and paper-based packaging order in a final rule effective 2026-03-09, and producers rejected a proposed natural grass sod order (36.49 percent in favor), after which AMS withdrew it (2025-05-29). AMS also acted in other directions at industry request: a final rule effective 2026-04-08 raised the Christmas tree board's administrative expense cap from 10 to 15 percent; a January 2026 hearing notice covers South Texas onion order amendments that would change the continuance threshold from two-thirds to a majority of voters and add paid promotion authority; and the House-passed farm bill (H.R. 7567) extends the dairy checkoff through 2031. AMS continued routine continuance referenda (Christmas tree, mango, blueberry, pecan, kiwifruit, tart cherry, Florida citrus and avocado, onion orders) and marketing order rules, including spearmint oil salable quantities. The 119th Congress bills on checkoffs found (H.R. 3516 and S. 1848, the Opportunities for Fairness in Farming Act of 2025) address lobbying contracts, conflicts of interest, transparency and audits, and the House text contains no termination or referendum provision.

timeline.event: Rep. Mace introduces H.R. 3516, the Opportunities for Fairness in Farming Act of 2025 (Sen. Lee's companion, S. 1848, was introduced 2025-05-21): it would bar large checkoff boards from contracting with groups that seek to influence agricultural policy, ban conflicts of interest and anticompetitive conduct, and require budget publication and audits; the House text has no referendum or termination provision.

AMS publishes a direct final rule removing 7 CFR part 1240, the referendum procedures for the proposed Natural Grass Sod Promotion, Research, and Information Order, after producers voted against the order (36.49 percent in favor); the rule calls itself deregulatory under Executive Order 14192 and the proposed order is withdrawn through a separate notice.

AMS publishes a rule on the Paper and Paper-Based Packaging Promotion, Research and Information Order titled as a continuance referendum and moratorium on assessment collection; the later termination rule says this notice suspended assessment collection with immediate effect, after a petition from more than 10 percent of eligible voters in January 2025.

AMS publishes a hearing notice (hearing set for 2026-02-03 and 2026-02-04) on industry-submitted amendments to the South Texas onion order, including changing the continuance referendum threshold from two-thirds of voting producers to a majority and adding marketing promotion authority; an interim final rule effective 2026-05-26 later suspends the 2026 continuance referendum until 2032, citing the overlap with this rulemaking.

AMS publishes a final rule terminating the paper and paper-based packaging order and removing 7 CFR part 1222, effective the same day, after a referendum on 2025-07-14 to 2025-07-25 in which about 73.5 percent of voters (about 90.4 percent of volume) favored ending it; the order had taken effect 2014-01-23 and collected about $21.2 million from 46 entities in 2024.

AMS publishes a final rule (effective 2026-04-08) amending the Christmas tree promotion order at the board's recommendation: the administrative expense cap rises from 10 to 15 percent, the board is renamed, and meeting and records rules change; the rule is exempt from Executive Order 14192.

The House passes H.R. 7567 (224 to 200); per CRS, it extends the National Dairy Promotion and Research Board's authority, which expires 2026-09-30 under current law, through 2031-09-30, and the Senate bill reauthorizes the dairy checkoff with minor wording differences.

AMS publishes notice of a second Christmas tree order continuance referendum (voting 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-16, about 1,200 eligible persons) because the May to June 2026 vote showed 49.83 percent support and had a shortened window with late ballots; if a majority does not favor continuing, USDA would follow the order's suspension and termination procedures.

title: Reduce and reform USDA marketing orders and checkoff programs
uncertainties: The stage remains a judgment: the paper packaging termination and the sod withdrawal reduced the count of programs, but each followed a producer petition or vote under existing law rather than a USDA initiative, so in_progress is a defensible alternative and diverged is arguable given the Christmas tree and South Texas onion actions. Absence of a USDA initiative rests on Federal Register API queries of AMS documents (promotion, research and information orders: 12 documents; marketing order termination and referendum: 13 and 14 documents, none terminating a marketing order and none proposing a new order), the Federal Register text of the documents cited, and web searches that returned older material (2020 beef order, 2021 to 2023 checkoff bills). Statements about the mango, blueberry, pecan, kiwifruit, tart cherry, citrus, avocado and onion referenda and the spearmint oil rule are title-level only. The CRS farm bill report was read for dairy provisions only (the first 100,000 of 139,275 characters), so other House or Senate checkoff provisions, for example in the horticulture title, were not fully reviewed; the Senate committee approved its bill 12 to 11 on 2026-09-16 and its checkoff content was not reviewed. Whether USDA has declined any new checkoff request was not found, and the S. 1848 text itself was not read (its press release and bibliographic record were). The Senate companion's introduction date is 2025-05-21 per GovInfo (the sponsor's release says 2025-05-22).
